meta.title: Who really said "The ends justify the means"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Machiavelli never wrote “the ends justify the means” — Wikiquote calls it his most common misquotation. The proverb’s real ancestor is Ovid.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The ends justify the means'?
meta.ogDescription: Not in The Prince, and not Machiavelli’s words. The nearest genuine line is Chapter XVIII; the phrase traces back to Ovid’s ‘exitus acta probat.’

answer.label: Not Machiavelli’s words — a proverb pinned on him
answer.sourceLine: The blunt line “the ends justify the means” appears nowhere in The Prince or Machiavelli’s other works — Wikiquote lists it under “Misattributed” as “the most common mis-quotation attributed to Machiavelli” ↗. The closest he actually wrote is a narrower observation in Chapter XVIII that people “judge by the result.” The proverb’s real literary ancestor is Ovid.

source.heading: What Machiavelli actually wrote

docMeta.dd: No — the exact phrase appears nowhere
The Prince, ch. XVIII — “one judges by the result”

source.excerpt: In the actions of all men, and especially of princes, which it is not prudent to challenge, one judges by the result. … Let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest, and he will be praised by everybody; because the vulgar are always taken by what a thing seems to be and by what comes of it.
trail: Wikiquote files the line under “Misattributed” ↗, calling it Machiavelli’s most common misquotation and stating it is never found in his works.

The nearest real passage is The Prince, ch. XVIII, where the Marriott translation has a prince’s means “always be considered honest” because people “judge by the result” ↗ — a comment on perception, not a maxim.
The sharper wording predates him: Ovid’s “exitus acta probat” (Heroides II.85) is glossed with “The ends justify the means” as a variant translation ↗.
source.cutTag: The real text vs. the slogan
source.excerptNote: The Prince, ch. XVIII (Marriott translation) — the closest genuine passage. Note it describes how people judge a ruler, and never states the slogan itself.

source.rightsNote: The English proverb “the ends justify the means” has no identifiable single author or first-publication work, so no copyright status can be asserted for the phrase itself. The genuine Chapter XVIII passage quoted here is from W. K. Marriott’s 1908 translation, which is public domain; Machiavelli’s original Italian (1513/1532) has been public domain for centuries.

author.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
author.heading: About Niccolò Machiavelli
author.metaLine: 1469–1527 · Florentine diplomat & author of The Prince
author.bio: Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, historian and political theorist whose 1513 treatise The Prince made his name a byword for cold, results-first statecraft. His actual argument in Chapter XVIII is subtler than the slogan attached to him: he observes that rulers are judged by outcomes, not that any outcome morally launders any method. That reputation for ruthlessness is exactly why the flattened proverb sticks to him.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is arguably the internet’s definitive Machiavelli misquote — short, cynical, and perfectly on-brand for his reputation, yet absent from everything he wrote.

items.why: The sentence appears in no edition of The Prince or his other writings. Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed,” calling it “the most common mis-quotation attributed to Machiavelli, which is never found within his works” ↗.

Even the thought is flattened. In Chapter XVIII Machiavelli says only that “one judges by the result” and that a victorious prince’s means “will always be considered honest” by the crowd — a description of public perception, not a doctrine that any end absolves any means ↗.

The nearest documented origin of the sentiment is Ovid’s “exitus acta probat” (Heroides II.85, c. 10 BC). Wikiquote lists “The ends justify the means” as one of its variant translations ↗ — centuries before Machiavelli.

misattribution.truthLine: It is an anonymous proverb, not a Machiavelli quotation; the man himself wrote a narrower point about being judged by results ↗, and the sharper phrasing traces back to Ovid.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Machiavelli
lead: The Prince’s reputation for cold pragmatism turned Machiavelli’s name into a magnet for any slogan about ruthless expediency — and “the ends justify the means” is the tidiest of them. But his actual claim in Chapter XVIII is descriptive, not a moral licence: he notes that observers “judge by the result,” so a prince who wins and holds his state will find “the means will always be considered honest” by the crowd.

That is a comment on how people react to success, not a philosophy that any goal excuses any method. The proverb flattens the hedge out of it — which is precisely why it travels so well and why it keeps getting hung on his name.
context.pull: He said people judge by results — not that results absolve you.
